title: A Real-Life Sea Monster? Rare Goblin Shark Spotted Alive for the First Time!
summary:
Have you ever heard of a goblin shark? It sounds like something from a scary movie, but it's real—and super rare. Until now, every time scientists saw one alive, it had been accidentally caught on a fishing line and brought to the surface, where it usually died soon after. But now, for the very first time, researchers have filmed healthy goblin sharks swimming freely in the deep, dark ocean!

These sharks are sometimes called 'living fossils' because their family has been around for 125 million years—that's way before the dinosaurs went extinct! They have a weird, long, flat snout and a jaw that can shoot forward to snatch prey. The new videos show one goblin shark near an underwater mountain close to Jarvis Island, and another along the steep slope of the Tonga Trench. The Tonga Trench shark was found nearly 700 meters deeper than anyone knew these sharks could live. That's like stacking seven Statues of Liberty on top of each other!

Before this, scientists thought goblin sharks only lived in certain parts of the Pacific, Atlantic, and Indian Oceans. But these two sightings in the Central Pacific show they travel much farther than we thought. The first video was actually recorded back in 2019 by a robot submarine named Hercules, but nobody realized it was a goblin shark until a student named Aaron Judah checked the old footage in 2025. He was shocked! Then in 2024, a baited camera on the seafloor captured another one. 'I never thought we'd see a goblin shark alive,' said Professor Alan Jamieson, who led the second expedition. 'It was amazing.'

Why does this matter? Knowing where these mysterious sharks live helps countries protect them. As Aaron Judah said, 'New discoveries like this show there is still so much to explore in our deep ocean home.' So next time you look at the ocean, remember: there might be a goblin shark lurking far below, waiting to be discovered!
why_it_matters: Discovering new deep-sea animals reminds us that our planet still holds secrets, and one day you might be the scientist to explore them.

background_read: The deep ocean is mostly unexplored. Scientists use robot submarines like Hercules (a machine that can dive very deep) to explore places humans can't go. The Tonga Trench is one of the deepest spots on Earth, and Jarvis Island is a remote U.S. territory in the Pacific.

WHAT: The first-ever video of healthy goblin sharks swimming freely in their deep-sea home
WHERE: Near Jarvis Island and the Tonga Trench in the Central Pacific Ocean
WHY: To learn where these rare sharks travel so countries can protect them

perspectives.description: This is amazing! It opens up a whole new understanding of where goblin sharks live and how they behave.
We must be careful not to damage or pollute these rare sharks' deep-sea homes while we explore.
Old video footage can still lead to big discoveries, so patience and curiosity are really valuable in science.
